This randomized clinical trial evaluated the effects of an eight-week online Mindfulness-Based Intervention (MBI), with weekly one-hour sessions, on psychological and biological markers of stress in 35 women with RPL. Participants were randomly assigned to either the MBI or standard care (control group) and assessed before and after the intervention through salivary biomarkers (cortisol, alpha-amylase, and Immunoglobulin A-IgA) and the validated questionnaires Depression, Anxiety and Stress Scale-21 (DASS-21) and Psychological General Well-Being Index (PGWB-I). No significant time × group interactions were observed for salivary biomarkers, including cortisol (p = 0.672), alpha-amylase (p = 0.342), and IgA (p = 0.148). Participants in the MBI group showed significant reductions in total DASS-21 (p = 0.018), depression (p = 0.026), and stress (p = 0.015) scores, whereas anxiety did not differ significantly between groups (p = 0.121). They also showed robust improvements in overall well-being (p < 0.001) and multiple PGWB-I domains. These findings suggest that MBI may improve self-reported psychological well-being in women with RPL; however, as no significant effects were observed in the primary biomarker outcomes, these secondary psychological findings should be considered exploratory and hypothesis-generating. However, these mechanisms can vary widely depending on the mindfulness-based intervention (MBI).</AbstractText><AbstractText Label="OBJECTIVE" NlmCategory="OBJECTIVE">To study possible mechanisms of action of 2 similar MBIs for pain.</AbstractText><AbstractText Label="DESIGN" NlmCategory="METHODS">We used data from our learning to apply mindfulness to pain (LAMP) pragmatic randomized controlled trial comparing usual care with virtual group or self-paced MBIs. The LAMP MBIs included education on adaptive pain behaviors and mindfulness and used shorter, less formal mindfulness practice than standard MBIs. We examined whether mindfulness, pain self-efficacy, pain catastrophizing, and stress mediated the treatment effects on 2 pain and 7 pain-related biopsychosocial outcomes at 10 weeks and 6 months using mediation models.</AbstractText><AbstractText Label="RESULTS" NlmCategory="RESULTS">The MBIs improved pain catastrophizing, pain self-efficacy, and mindfulness but did not affect perceived stress. meditation is an evidence-based therapy for pain. We examined how the effectiveness of a mindfulness-based intervention (MBI) for pain was affected by the user’s mindfulness skills, stress, ability to feel effective in dealing with pain, and how much they “catastrophized” pain. That is, we examined these 4 issues as potential reasons for why the MBI worked for pain and pain-related psychosocial issues. We used data from our learning to apply mindfulness to pain (LAMP) study that compared veterans getting the MBI or veterans getting only their usual healthcare. Our LAMP MBI included education on adaptive pain behaviors and mindfulness and used shorter, less formal mindfulness practice than standard MBIs. We found that the degree to which veterans catastrophized about their pain or felt they were effective in dealing with their pain greatly affected how much the LAMP MBIs worked on all health conditions we examined—their pain interference, pain intensity, physical functioning, social functioning, anxiety, fatigue, sleep disturbance, depression, and post-traumatic stress disorder. Veterans’ stress did not affect how well the LAMP MBI worked, but their mindfulness slightly did for half the health conditions. This study improves our understanding of why a pain-focused MBI can affect pain and important pain-related outcomes.</AbstractText><CopyrightInformation>Published by Oxford University Press on behalf ValidYN="Y">10.1002/pon.70610</ELocationID><Abstract><AbstractText Label="BACKGROUND" NlmCategory="BACKGROUND">Patients with cervical cancer or High-Grade Squamous Intraepithelial Lesion (HSIL) often experience mental problems such as anxiety and depression. Online mindfulness-based interventions offer accessible mental health support. However, evidence for cervical cancer or HSIL patients remains scarce, and evaluations often rely solely on self-reported scales, with a lack of neurophysiological assessments. This study aimed to assess the effectiveness of a 6-week online mindfulness-based intervention on mental health outcomes in this population by using scales, with exploratory frontal electroencephalogram (EEG) biomarkers as supplementary neurophysiological indicators.</AbstractText><AbstractText Label="METHODS" NlmCategory="METHODS">A single-center randomized controlled trial enrolling 151 cervical cancer or HSIL patients was conducted. The intervention group received a 6-week online mindfulness-based intervention, while the control group received general mental health education. Primary outcomes were depressive and anxiety symptoms assessed by validated scales. Frontal EEG metrics were collected as exploratory supplementary neurophysiological indicators. Assessments were conducted at baseline and post-intervention. Independent samples t-tests and Mann-Whitney U tests were used for intergroup comparisons, with Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction applied to control for multiple testing.</AbstractText><AbstractText Label="RESULTS" NlmCategory="RESULTS">A total of 149 patients completed the study. After the intervention, the intervention showed significantly lower symptoms of depression (t = 12.238, FDR-q < 0.001), anxiety (t = 11.150, FDR-q < 0.001), and higher levels of resilience, mindfulness, and perceived social support than the control group. Exploratory EEG analysis revealed that the intervention group exhibited higher relative theta and alpha power, higher time-domain standard deviation, and lower relative beta and gamma power than the control group.</AbstractText><AbstractText Label="CONCLUSION" NlmCategory="CONCLUSIONS">This study demonstrates that a 6-week online mindfulness-based intervention effectively alleviates depressive and anxiety symptoms among patients with cervical cancer or HSIL. Exploratory EEG findings provide preliminary neurophysiological support for these psychological benefits, though further validation with larger samples is warranted.</AbstractText><AbstractText Label="TRIAL REGISTRATION" NlmCategory="BACKGROUND">The trial was prospectively registered on the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (ID: ChiCTR2400087926, https://www.chictr.org.cn/) on August 07, 2024.</AbstractText><CopyrightInformation>© 2026 John Wiley & Sons Ltd. EIdType="pii" ValidYN="Y">S0967-5868(26)00454-6</ELocationID><Abstract><AbstractText Label="AIMS" NlmCategory="OBJECTIVE">We aim to investigate the clinical application effect of multimodal analgesia (MMA) combined with mindfulness-based stress reduction (MBSR) therapy in patients following spinal fusion surgery, analyze its impacts on post spinal-fusion surgery pain control, rehabilitation progress, and sleep quality, thereby providing evidence to inform comprehensive postoperative care protocols.</AbstractText><AbstractText Label="METHODS" NlmCategory="METHODS">In this single-center, parallel-group randomized controlled trial, 124 patients were allocated 1:1 to an intervention group (MMA plus MBSR, n = 62) or a control group (conventional analgesia, n = 62) with concealed allocation and blinded outcome assessment. The results were compared between the two groups, including: pain intensity measured by the visual analogue scale (VAS) at 6 h, 12 h, 24 h, 48 h, and 72 h postoperatively; analgesic drug utilization (rate of use, number of rescue doses, duration of use); rehabilitation indicators (time to first ambulation, length of hospital stay, spinal function recovery score); sleep quality by the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI); and psychological status evaluated by the Self-Rating Anxiety Scale (SAS) and Self-Rating Depression Scale (SDS). Cumulative opioid consumption expressed as oral morphine equivalents, adverse events, and treatment adherence were also recorded, and repeatedly measured outcomes were analyzed with linear mixed-effects models.</AbstractText><AbstractText Label="RESULTS" NlmCategory="RESULTS">Postoperative VAS scores were significantly lower in the intervention group at all measured time points (6 h, 12 h, 24 h, 48 h and 72 h) compared to the control group (all P < 0.001), with a significant group-by-time interaction (P < 0.001). The intervention group also demonstrated a lower rate of analgesic drug use, fewer rescue doses, and a shorter duration of analgesic use, together with lower cumulative oral morphine equivalents. Rehabilitation outcomes were superior in the intervention group, as evidenced by a shorter time to first ambulation, reduced hospital stay, and a higher spinal function recovery score. At one and two weeks postoperatively, PSQI scores were significantly lower in the intervention group. Furthermore, SAS and SDS scores at two weeks were lower in the intervention group compared to the control group. Adverse events were less frequent in the intervention group.</AbstractText><AbstractText Label="CONCLUSION" NlmCategory="CONCLUSIONS">In this single-center trial with short follow-up, the combination of MMA and MBSR therapy effectively alleviates postoperative pain, reduces analgesic use, enhances early rehabilitation and functional recovery, and improves sleep quality while mitigating anxiety and depression. However, because the design was not intended to separate the independent effects of MMA and MBSR, these findings require confirmation in multicenter trials.</AbstractText><CopyrightInformation>Copyright © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. ValidYN="Y">10.1371/journal.pone.0357906</ELocationID><Abstract><AbstractText Label="INTRODUCTION" NlmCategory="BACKGROUND">Nearly 80% of healthcare providers experience adverse psychological symptoms (e.g., depression, burnout, sleep disturbance) stemming from workplace stressors. Elevated levels of stress have been associated with unfavorable occupational, patient, and provider-related outcomes, imposing a heavy burden on a strained system. Given the impact of stress on both employee and patient health, effective interventions are urgently needed to reduce distress and promote well-being among healthcare professionals. Mindfulness-based interventions show promise for addressing these challenges. We developed a six-week, remotely delivered mindfulness intervention, the Building Emotional Strength Training (BEST) program, based on the Buddhist Four Immeasurables practice to cultivate the distinct emotional qualities of loving-kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity. The present study aims to evaluate the feasibility and efficacy of a Four Immeasurables-based mindfulness intervention on perceived stress (primary outcome), burnout, depressive symptoms, and inflammatory biomarkers, while enhancing psychological well-being and sleep quality (secondary outcomes) in physicians. We will also investigate potential mediators of intervention effects, including compassion, positive affect, equanimity, and mindfulness.</AbstractText><AbstractText Label="METHOD" NlmCategory="METHODS">We will enroll 90 full-time physicians in a remote, two-arm randomized controlled trial with 1:1 allocation to either the meditation intervention or waitlist control. Participants will complete self-report questionnaires and provide blood samples at baseline, mid-course, and post-intervention to assess outcomes and mediators.</AbstractText><AbstractText Label="DISCUSSION" NlmCategory="CONCLUSIONS">The project aims to advance the study of mindfulness-based interventions that reduce distress and promote well-being through practices that cultivate prosocial and altruistic feelings toward oneself and others. While mindfulness interventions have gained considerable interest, none have specifically drawn from the Four Immeasurables practice to target loving-kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity. This novel investigation could expand our understanding of practices that foster kindness and compassion to reduce distress in an at-risk population.</AbstractText><AbstractText Label="TRIAL REGISTRATION" NlmCategory="BACKGROUND">ClinicalTrials.gov NCT07283744, registered on 2025/10/14. The fast-growing mobile health services industry has provided new opportunities for workplace mental health.</AbstractText><AbstractText Label="OBJECTIVE">This randomized controlled trial examined the effectiveness of <i>Neurum</i> (Neurum Limited), a smartphone-based intervention tool featuring ecological momentary assessments and interventions that aims to reduce workplace stress in real-time and real-world settings.</AbstractText><AbstractText Label="METHODS">A total of 201 working adults were recruited for a 4-week smartphone-based intervention that incorporated cognitive behavioral therapy, mindfulness exercises, and self-regulation exercises delivered on <i>Neurum</i>. A simple randomization procedure was used. Participants in the intervention group were encouraged to log mood journals, complete mental health exercises, and provide user feedback whenever applicable. The key outcome was measured by the Depression, Anxiety, and Stress Scale-21 items (DASS-21; Cronbach α=0.87).</AbstractText><AbstractText Label="RESULTS">The intervention group consisted of 102 participants, while the control group consisted of 99 participants. More participants dropped out from the intervention group (n=21) than from the control group (n=2; <i>χ</i><sup>2</sup><sub>1</sub>=18.259; <i>P</i><.001). The final sample consisted of 178 participants (male: 85/178, 47.8%; female: 93/178, 52.2%; mean age of 34.65, SD 7.67 y). Analyses revealed that after the 4-week intervention, the DASS-21 scores decreased in the intervention group (mean difference [MD]<sub>post-pre intervention</sub>=-14.518) but increased in the control group (MD<sub>post-pre intervention</sub>=3.319; <i>F</i><sub>1,176</sub>=59.358, <i>P</i><.001; <i>η<sup>2</sup></i>=0.252). This effect was largely led by stress reduction (<i>F</i><sub>1,176</sub>=64.679, <i>P</i><.001; for the intervention group, MD<sub>post-pre intervention</sub>=-6.692, while for the control group, MD<sub>post-pre intervention</sub>=2.000). On average, participants completed 6.27 (SD 9.4) exercises and provided 9.74 (SD 18.2) mood journal logs, with a daily engagement of 4.95 (SD 6.89) minutes. However, the associations between the changes in DASS-21 scores and the numbers of exercises or mood journal logs did not reach statistical significance.</AbstractText><AbstractText Label="CONCLUSIONS">This study primarily established the effectiveness of <i>Neurum</i> in alleviating depression, anxiety, and stress symptoms in noninstitutionalized working adults, with a satisfactory user retention rate. Despite potential health-related culture differences, <i>Neurum</i> contributed to evidence-based digital health in nonclinical settings for timely needs and general accessibility as an alternative to traditional, face-to-face, and high-cost mental health services. Future directions involving a personalized approach in online mental health services were discussed.</AbstractText><CopyrightInformation>© Sisi Li, Lik Hang Lincoln Lo, Chiu Yi Charlie Lau, Megan Lam, Meanne Chan.
